case_name: Reserve Bank Of India v N. C. Paliwal & Others
facts: The Reserve Bank of India was originally constituted to regulate the issue of bank notes and keep reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India.
In course of time, other functions were added as a result of various statutes passed by Parliament to meet economic needs.

The administrative machinery of the Reserve Bank for carrying out these diverse functions was divided into five groups of departments: General Side, Department of Banking Operations, Development and Industrial Finance, Agricultural Credit Department, Economic Department, and Department of Statistics.
Recruitment to these different groups of departments was made on a common basis, but each group was treated as a separate unit for determining seniority and promotion.
There were two grades of clerks in each group: Grade I and Grade II. Pay scales and conditions of service were the same for both grades.
Automatic promotion from Grade II to Grade I was possible, with an additional officiating allowance of Rs. 25 per month.
Some employees in the general departments were non-graduates, while those in the specialized departments were invariably graduates.
There were also several categories of non-clerical posts in both general and specialized departments.
issues: Whether the Combined Seniority Scheme issued by the Reserve Bank was valid
Whether employees in the general departments should have equal confirmation and promotional opportunities as those in the specialized departments
petitioner_arguments: The Association argued that all promotions should be made strictly according to combined seniority, regardless of department.

The Reserve Bank sought to justify maintaining separate seniority lists for various departments on the ground that work in each department was becoming more special and inter-transferability was undesirable.
respondent_arguments: The Reserve Bank argued that it was desirable to group employees in a particular category serving in different departments at one centre together for the purpose of being considered for promotion, but this would not affect the interests of the bank or efficiency.
The National Tribunal observed that it is desirable to maintain a common seniority list for employees in a particular category serving in different departments at one centre.
court_reasoning: The Court approved the observations of the National Tribunal, which were endorsed by this Court in All India Bank Employees Association v. Reserve Bank of India [1966] 1 S.C.R. 25.
The Court noted that the Reserve Bank took the first step towards equalising confirmation and promotional opportunities by introducing the Optee Scheme of 1965.
holding: The judgment of the High Court allowing Writ Petition No. 690/72 filed by some employees of the Reserve Bank challenging the validity of the Combined Seniority Scheme was upheld.
The appeals were allowed, and the judgment of the High Court was confirmed.
